findings.message: Phase 4 states the bundle builder 'regenerates git history from scratch' on every build, but Phase 7 promises collaborators a 'natural pull-to-update path'. If the bundle history is regenerated from a new detached root on every release, collaborators will encounter 'fatal: refusing to merge unrelated histories' during `git pull` and will be unable to update their instances. The scrubbed branch must maintain a continuous history.

Phase 2 mandates 'parent-dir-fsync' for atomic writes. Node.js on Windows does not support calling fsync on a directory file descriptor (it typically throws EBADF or EPERM). Relying on this POSIX-specific behavior for the durability primitives will instantly break the durability cluster and the Phase-1 pinning suite on Windows.

Phase 6 moves the 10-minute status format entirely to the engine ('never requested of the agent in prompts'). By mechanically emitting a timer-based status without the agent's semantic input, the system loses the agent's contextual self-reflection on its progress, explicitly regressing the 'narration invariants' and failing to behave identically to the author's instance.

Phase 3 proposes opening the browser with the token in the URL fragment. Passing the token as a command-line argument to launch the browser (e.g., `xdg-open http://localhost/#token`) leaks the bootstrap token to the OS process table. Any local process or unprivileged user running `ps` can read the token before the claim endpoint expires it.

Phase 4 introduces a 'short human spot-check checklist' as part of the leak-scan gate, yet mandates this gate runs synchronously in 'Scrub-as-CI' on 'every main-branch change'. A manual human gating step in the CI pipeline will block the matrix and halt all automated builds, breaking continuous integration.

The leak-scan gate checks for secrets, absolute paths, and specific string patterns, but it cannot algorithmically detect proprietary business logic, datasets, or real project code embedded within test fixtures. Relying solely on these mechanical pattern scans risks silently leaking the author's intellectual property in the scrubbed bundle.

Phase 4 mandates regenerating git history from scratch to achieve the scrubbed bundle required by NS (1). However, a repository with a rewritten, synthetic history shares no common ancestor with the upstream private remote. This mechanically breaks the 'pull-to-update' path introduced in Phase 7, trapping the collaborator on their initial version or forcing them to manually resolve unrelated histories on every update.

Phase 3 forces a 'TLS-or-refuse' policy for non-loopback binds to satisfy NS (3). Yet it also recommends Tailscale/SSH as the sanctioned remote-access answer. Tailscale binds to a non-loopback IP (the overlay network) but provides its own transport security. Forcing application-level TLS on an overlay network—while explicitly deferring TLS certificate automation—introduces fatal UX friction and breaks the very exposure path you are sanctioning.

Phase 2 attempts to maintain durability (NS 5) via 'temp+fsync+rename+parent-dir-fsync'. On Windows, renaming over an existing file is not inherently atomic in the POSIX sense and often throws locking errors if the target is being read by another process (e.g., an indexer or another agent). Blindly porting POSIX durability primitives to Windows will introduce intermittent state corruptions and directly violate the 'no durability regression' criterion.

Phase 5 introduces a 'telemetry-free default' for collaborators. However, NS (4) strictly demands the agent trio 'behaves identically to the author's'. If the author's system depends on telemetry for narration, reporting, or loop invariants, disabling it by default creates a silent behavioral fork, undermining the guarantee of identical governance and execution.

Phase 4 mandates regenerating git history from scratch for every bundle. Phase 7 promises a 'natural pull-to-update path' for collaborators using git pull against the private remote. These are mechanically incompatible. If the bundle's history is regenerated from scratch on every release, the collaborator's local repository will share no commit ancestry with the updated remote, causing git pull to fail with a fatal unrelated histories error. You must either maintain a persistent scrubbed branch with continuous history, or abandon git pull for updates.

Phase 2 mandates 'parent-dir-fsync' for atomic writes as part of the OS-abstraction layer. While opening and fsyncing a parent directory is standard POSIX practice for ensuring a directory entry is durably written to disk, Windows Node.js does not permit this; attempting to fsync a directory handle natively throws an EPERM/EACCES error. This completely breaks the required durability primitives on one of the primary target OSes out of the gate.

Phase 3 enforces 'TLS-or-refuse' when binding to non-loopback interfaces, while simultaneously sanctioning Tailscale as the remote-access answer. Tailscale provides its own virtual IP (non-loopback) and handles end-to-end encryption natively. Forcing TLS on top of Tailscale requires the collaborator to provision a custom TLS certificate for their Tailscale IP. This introduces massive friction, contradicting the zero-friction onboarding goal, and will push users to abandon the sanctioned secure path.
